articles.title: 2 Election Commissioners complained against poll panel officer, but Cabinet Secretariat took no action: RTI
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat did not take any action on complaints filed by two election commissioners against an officer in the Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat did not take any action on complaints filed by two election commissioners against an officer in the Election Commission, saying the letters were written in their “individual capacity” and did not represent the poll panel as a whole, according to documents released in response to an RTI application.Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had separately written to Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan on July 29, raising concerns about the conduct of senior deputy election commissioner Maneesh Garg, an IAS officer appointed to the Commission by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) on September 2, 2024.The letters were provided in an RTI response to activist Commodore Lokesh K Batra (retd).The Indian Express had reported in September that the two Election Commissioners approached the Cabinet Secretary after Garg issued a work allocation order that they believed could concentrate powers over changes to voter records at the central level, instead of allowing officials at the state level to handle them.In a statement on September 26, the Election Commission said the work allocation orders issued by Garg were never implemented following directions from the two Commissioners.The poll panel also said the complaints concerned an officer on deputation and not matters related to policy or the IT division.What did the Election Commissioners allegeAccording to a Cabinet note included in the RTI response, both Commissioners alleged that Garg had issued an order changing the work allocation of officers senior or equivalent to him after taking charge as the link officer of the deputy election commissioner (Administration).The Commissioners said the changes were made without consulting the Commission or the officers concerned. They also alleged that Garg acted despite repeated oral and written instructions against making such changes without prior discussion or approval from the Commission."Both the ECs have stated that Shri Garg, after assuming the charge as link officer of DEC (Admn), has issued an order regarding work allocation of equivalent and senior officers to him without discussing the revised work allocation with the Commission or the officers concerned. Further, the aforementioned ECs have stated that this has happened despite repeated oral and written instructions to all concerned officers against taking such actions without prior discussion/approval of the Commission," the Cabinet note said.The two Commissioners alleged that Garg's actions violated the chief election commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.Joshi also said that when he sought the relevant file from the Administration Division, it was not provided to him.Why did the Cabinet Secretariat refrain from taking actionA Cabinet note prepared on August 3 proposed seeking the chief election commissioner's opinion on the complaints."In this connection, we may request the chief election commissioner for his opinion on the issue. Accordingly, a draft DO is put up for approval, please."However, a subsequent note dated August 4 said taking action on complaints from individual Election Commissioners without an official communication from the Commission as a whole could be seen as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body."The Commission is a Constitutional Body and is insulated from executive interference by design to ensure that it functions independently and in a transparent manner. The working and functioning of the Commission are governed by the rules and guidelines of the Election Commission. The above communications are from the Election Commissioners in their individual capacity and, while they must be taken with due seriousness, they cannot be seen as a formal communication from the Commission as a whole," the note said.It added that although Garg had been appointed by the ACC, he was now an officer of the Election Commission, and his work and conduct were governed by the poll panel's rules and guidelines.The note also referred to Section 18 of the 2023 Act, which states that the Commission should conduct its business unanimously as far as possible, with any differences of opinion settled by a majority decision."Election Commissioners have sent these communications for appropriate action; however, in the absence of any official communication from the Commission as a whole, any action at this stage may be inappropriate. It may also be construed as interference in the functioning of the Constitutional Body. Hence, it would be appropriate to send acknowledgement to both Election Commissioners with a copy to PPS to CEC for information of CEC," the note said.Cabinet Secretary acknowledges complaintsThe draft note signed by Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan was also marked to the secretary of the department of personnel and training and the establishment officer to keep the matter on record.The note said this would "enable it to be taken into account in future decision-making regarding the officer".Somanathan also signed an acknowledgement letter confirming receipt of the complaints and sent copies to both election commissioners.The letters were acknowledged on August 5, 2026, with copies marked to the department of personnel and training, the Establishment Officer and the office of the chief election commissioner.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dallas built an underground freight railway in 1924 to move goods through downtown; the Santa Fe tunnels later became disconnected from the main rail line
articles.summary: Beneath downtown Dallas lies a little-known chapter of the city’s transportation history: a network of railroad tunnels built to move freight through the
articles.body: Beneath downtown Dallas lies a little-known chapter of the city’s transportation history: a network of railroad tunnels built to move freight through the central business district without relying on a maze of surface tracks. Beginning in 1924, the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe Railway developed a complex of 4 freight-terminal buildings connected by underground tracks. The arrangement allowed freight to reach warehouses in the heart of the city while reducing the surface railroad lines that had obstructed downtown traffic. The freight operation eventually fell into disuse after World War II, and construction of the Dallas Convention Centre later severed the tunnels from the main rail line. Records maintained by the City of Dallas and the National Register of Historic Places document the complex, which formed part of a broader effort to reorganise transportation and commercial activity in a rapidly growing city.Dallas freight tunnels and the Kessler PlanBy the early 20th century, Dallas was served by multiple railroads, each operating its own stations, tracks and freight facilities. The resulting network created congestion in the downtown street grid, where railroad lines competed with road traffic and pedestrians for space. George Kessler’s 1910 city plan proposed reorganising the railroad system, removing troublesome tracks and improving the city’s streets and circulation. Dallas Union Terminal, now known as Dallas Union Station, opened in 1916, although some later Dallas landmark documentation gives 1917 as the year of its completion. The consolidated station replaced the need for several separate passenger depots. The National Register record for Dallas Union Terminal identifies 1916 as a significant year in the station’s history.With passenger services consolidated, the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe Railway developed a new freight complex on adjoining downtown blocks. Construction began in 1924, according to the City of Dallas’s historic preservation record for Santa Fe Building No. 1. The complex was designed to centralise the railroad’s transfer and warehousing operations while removing the need for an extensive network of surface tracks. The buildings combined offices, warehouses and freight-related facilities. Designed by Dallas architect Lloyd R. Whitson, the buildings served businesses that relied on rail transport to receive, store and distribute merchandise. The project reflected Dallas’s role as a major commercial centre in the Southwest.How the Santa Fe freight tunnels workedThe Santa Fe complex comprised 4 buildings arranged across several downtown blocks, extending from the area around Commerce Street south toward Young Street. Underground railroad tracks connected the buildings to a central line that emerged farther south and linked the freight operation to the main railroad connection. The tunnels allowed freight cars to reach the warehouses below street level rather than moving through a sprawling arrangement of surface tracks. The City of Dallas’s record for the Santa Fe II Freight Terminal and Warehouse confirms that an underground tunnel connected the 4 buildings and that a special steamless locomotive was devised for the system. The underground arrangement made it possible to move freight within the complex while reducing disruption to streets above. The Santa Fe Terminal Buildings No. 1 and No. 2 National Register documentation records the complex’s architectural and transportation significance. The tunnels were not simply pedestrian passages: they formed part of a working freight railway designed to connect warehouses and facilitate the transfer of goods.Why the freight tunnels fell into disuseThe underground freight operation did not remain in service indefinitely. The One Main Place landmark nomination prepared for the Dallas Landmark Commission states that the Santa Fe terminals fell into disuse after World War II. Construction of the Dallas Convention Centre eventually severed the tunnels from the main rail line, leaving the underground freight system disconnected from the railway network it had served. The nomination is available through the City of Dallas’s historic preservation records. The buildings subsequently followed different paths. Building No. 3, which housed cold-storage facilities, was demolished in 1988, according to accounts of the Santa Fe complex. Building No. 4, the smallest of the four structures, was left abandoned for years before being converted into an Aloft hotel in 2009, according to published accounts of the complex. Other surviving buildings have been adapted for new uses, while remnants of the underground railway remain associated with the surviving structures.Records differ on the address and designation history of the Santa Fe complex’s second warehouse. The National Register documentation identifies Building No. 2 at 1118 Jackson Street, while the City of Dallas identifies Santa Fe II at 1122 Jackson Street and records its landmark designation in 1998 and National Register listing in 2004. The city’s Santa Fe II landmark nomination also identifies Warehouse No. 2 at 1118 Jackson Street, suggesting that the records may refer to the same building despite the conflicting addresses and listing dates. The discrepancy should not be resolved by treating them as separate buildings.Other underground passages beneath downtown DallasThe Santa Fe freight tunnels were part of a wider history of efforts to move certain activities below street level. A tunnel constructed beneath Main Street in 1913 connected the Adolphus Hotel and the Busch Building, primarily to link the hotel’s large power plant with the neighbouring building. At Union Station, an underground passage replaced an overhead walkway in 1947. These projects served purposes different from the Santa Fe freight railway, illustrating the range of functions that underground connections served in downtown Dallas.Another example emerged with the Mercantile complex. The Mercantile National Bank building, completed in 1943, was a major addition to the downtown business district. The City of Dallas’s preservation record documents the bank building’s history. A later landmark nomination for One Main Place describes an underground pedestrian connection associated with the Mercantile complex, alongside underground parking and freight facilities. Historic records differ on the parking structure’s precise date and configuration, so those details should not be treated as settled.The private Main Place superblock projectIn the 1960s, developers pursued a more ambitious vision for downtown Dallas through the Main Place superblock project. It was a private development rather than a municipal tunnel proposal. The project was initially conceived by Columbia University’s School of Architecture and refined into a buildable design by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Its plans envisioned a large development combining office buildings, retail areas, pedestrian connections, freight facilities, roadways and plazas. One Main Place, built between 1965 and 1968, was the only building completed from the proposed three-phase development. The remaining phases were abandoned because of a lack of financing, according to the City of Dallas’s landmark record and its One Main Place landmark nomination.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2020, a Portland man began rebuilding his 800-square-foot backyard with ping-pong and a hot tub; after spending $48,412, he had brought in about $85,000 from hourly rentals by 2025
articles.summary: When Rob Nachbar bought his Portland, Oregon, home in 2015, the backyard was little more than a patch of grass with a hot tub.
articles.body: When Rob Nachbar bought his Portland, Oregon, home in 2015, the backyard was little more than a patch of grass with a hot tub. By 2019, the grass was worn out, and an early redesign using pea gravel and flagstone made the space even less usable. Then the pandemic arrived, giving Nachbar and his family both time at home and a reason to rethink how they lived outdoors. What followed was a five-year, hand-built transformation of an 800-square-foot yard into a covered, colourful entertainment space called Pong Springs. According to Realtor.com, the project cost $48,412, while Axios reported that by 2025 the backyard had generated about $85,000 through hourly rentals on Swimply.The result is not a conventional garden makeover. Nachbar turned a small 20-by-40-foot yard into four covered zones: a hot tub area, a fire deck, a pavilion with a ping-pong table and a grill deck. The design leans into bright colours, neon lighting and a playful Palm Springs-inspired mood, making the space feel more like a private mini resort than a typical suburban backyard.The backyard began as a problemNachbar initially tried to improve the yard with help from a landscaper friend, but the removal of all the grass and its replacement with pea gravel created a practical problem for a family with a young child. During the pandemic, he watched his wife’s five-year-old daughter kicking gravel around the yard and worried that a stone could break a window. That moment convinced him that the space needed to be completely rebuilt rather than simply redecorated, as per the reports.The first step was physically demanding. Nachbar and others removed the gravel, dug out the yard by hand and dealt with a pile of displaced soil that grew into an eight-foot mound. After compacting and levelling the ground, they installed artificial turf, a choice that eliminated the need to mow a very small lawn and created a cleaner base for the rest of the project. From there, the project developed without a rigid master plan. Nachbar had been collecting wooden pallets to build a deck, but he soon realised those materials would not last. A builder friend helped him create stronger structures using pressure-treated lumber, including a cantilevered fire deck and grill deck topped with polycarbonate roofing. The hot tub structure came last, completing a backyard where nearly every area except the walkways is covered.Why covering the yard matteredPortland’s wet climate shaped many of the design decisions. Nachbar covered most of the yard so that rain would not prevent the family from using the hot tub, fire area, grill space or ping-pong pavilion. The roofs allow the backyard to be used throughout the year, except during snow, and turned a small outdoor area into a set of weather-resistant rooms.Privacy was another priority. The property is surrounded by neighbours on every side, and the rear neighbour previously had a clear view into the yard. Nachbar added cedar privacy walls and bamboo planters, which filled in within about a year to create a more enclosed and intimate setting. He said the space is now private on all sides, even though nearby sounds can still be heard.The finishing touches gave Pong Springs its personality. Nachbar added extensive lighting, including neon signs, and embraced a deliberately kitschy, colourful aesthetic. A friend coined the name after seeing the artificial turf and ping-pong table, combining the game with the Palm Springs-inspired look that Nachbar and his family enjoyed.The $48,412 renovation budgetRealtor.com detailed the spending across the project, which Nachbar financed in cash and spread over five years rather than completing in one burst. The largest single expense was the hot tub at $11,900, followed by structures and carpentry at $10,990. Other costs included hardscaping, electrical work, heating and a fireplace, outdoor furniture, gardening, accessories, artificial turf and a kegerator.It was reported that Nachbar did much of the work himself, including running a natural gas line across the property after learning from online videos. He hired a company to install an additional electrical subpanel, while a friend with electrical experience handled much of the remaining wiring. He acknowledged that the project involved mistakes, including choosing a grout between flagstone pavers that later became crumbly, but said doing the work personally saved a significant amount of money.Turning a private yard into rental incomeThe rental idea began during the pandemic, when public pools were closed. A neighbour told Nachbar about Swimply, a platform that lets owners rent private pools and outdoor amenities by the hour. After booking a Swimply pool for his own family, he began wondering whether his backyard could work as a rental space too. The answer was 'yes'. Pong Springs is listed on Swimply and attracts guests looking for unusual places to gather, including bachelorette parties, date nights and themed watch parties. Nachbar added a projector and a pull-down screen, which helped the space become popular for Love Island viewing parties, football gatherings and other social events.The income has been meaningful. Nachbar told Axios that he had generated around $85,000 over the previous couple of years, describing the rental business as a steady side income that essentially pays the household mortgage. In the Realtor.com interview, he said the backyard had earned $106,000 in total over five years, or roughly $20,000 to $21,000 annually.How the bookings workRentals are booked by the hour, with a two-hour minimum. A busy weekend may include two reservations each day, while a typical month brings 10 to 15 bookings. Nachbar deliberately blocks many dates so his family can still enjoy the backyard, meaning the space is not constantly available to strangers.Demand is seasonal rather than uniform. He said the yard is busiest in spring and autumn, while fewer people seek a hot tub experience during July. The covered design helps reduce weather-related cancellations, but the appeal of an outdoor hot tub and fire deck still rises and falls with Portland’s cooler months.A wider rental trendNachbar’s backyard fits into a broader shift in how people use private amenities. Axios reported that Swimply has expanded beyond summer pool rentals with a winter category called Igloos, featuring about 1,500 listings nationwide for hourly rental. The platform said nearly 100 hosts in a beta programme between September 2024 and May 2025 each earned more than $10,000, with some top earners approaching $100,000 in revenue.The idea is simple: a costly home feature such as a pool, sauna or hot tub can become a source of income when it is rented to people who want the experience without the expense or upkeep of ownership. For guests, it offers a private alternative to crowded public facilities. For hosts, it can turn an underused backyard into a small hospitality business.Nachbar’s experience shows that the opportunity does not require a huge property. His yard is only 800 square feet, yet careful coverage, privacy screening, flexible seating and a distinctive theme helped it stand out. The project also illustrates the trade-off behind such ventures: the income did not appear overnight, and it came after years of construction, maintenance and hosting responsibilities.For the Nachbar family, though, the investment has delivered more than money. The backyard is now a low-maintenance place for their own gatherings, a private retreat in a dense neighbourhood and a rental space that pays a substantial share of the household bills.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A limited-edition steel watch by Finnish maker Kari Voutilainen entered a New York auction with a top estimate of $240,000; it sold for $1,016,000, more than four times that figure, in an October 2026 sale
articles.summary: A rare stainless-steel watch by independent watchmaker Kari Voutilainen sold for $1.016 million at a Phillips auction in New York on October 9, 2026,
articles.body: A rare stainless-steel watch by independent watchmaker Kari Voutilainen sold for $1.016 million at a Phillips auction in New York on October 9, 2026, substantially exceeding its highest estimate of $240,000. The timepiece, a Voutilainen 28Sport Limited Edition numbered 5 of 8, was offered by its original owner and sold for more than four times its upper estimate of $240,000. According to the official Phillips auction listing, the watch featured a blue guilloché dial surrounding a black onyx centre and came with its certificate and original presentation box. The result highlights the demand for rare watches made by independent horologists, particularly pieces distinguished by limited production and detailed craftsmanship.A rare watch far exceeds its estimateThe watch was lot 22 in Phillips Watches Online: The New York Sessions Fall 2026. The auction house estimated it at $120,000 to $240,000, but it ultimately sold for $1,016,000, including the buyer’s premium. The result was particularly notable because the final price exceeded the top estimate by $776,000. It was more than four times the highest estimate, making the watch one of the standout results of the online sale.According to Phillips, the watch dates to around 2021 and was consigned by its original owner. It was presented with a Voutilainen certificate booklet, instruction manual, polishing cloth, travel case, additional strap, outer packaging and fitted presentation box. The sale was part of an auction featuring 88 lots of watches. Barrington Watch Winders, which reported on the result, noted that the 28Sport was among the sale's most striking performers. The auction's result also demonstrated how a particular combination of rarity, design and maker reputation can push a collectible timepiece well beyond its estimate.What makes the Voutilainen 28Sport distinctiveThe 28Sport is different from the traditional dress watches and complicated timepieces for which Voutilainen is known. The model combines a relatively sporty design with the careful finishing associated with independent Swiss watchmaking. The model was introduced in 2020 in limited runs of eight stainless-steel watches and eight titanium examples. The auctioned watch was number 5 of the eight steel pieces, making it part of a very small production series.Its 39-millimetre stainless-steel case has distinctive downturned, teardrop-shaped lugs. The dial is one of its most recognisable features, combining a glossy black onyx centre with a blue, engine-turned guilloché hour track. Orange indexes add contrast, while luminous details help make the time visible in low light. Phillips described the particular dial configuration as possibly one of only two examples across the limited edition. This additional rarity may have contributed to the strong auction result, although the final price alone does not establish which factor influenced bidders most.Hand-finished mechanics behind the designBeyond its appearance, the watch contains an in-house manually wound calibre 28 movement with 21 jewels. Phillips' catalogue notes describe a large balance wheel and a distinctive balance-spring arrangement combining a Phillips overcoil on the outer curve with a Grossmann curve on the inner section. The movement is finished with traditional decorative techniques, including Côtes de Genève and perlage on the base plate. These details reflect the time and specialist skill involved in producing a watch in a small independent workshop.Voutilainen's approach differs from the mass production of many large watch brands. His watches are associated with hand-fabricated components, careful assembly and detailed finishing. In the luxury watch market, such work can make an individual piece appealing to collectors who value mechanical construction as much as brand recognition.What the million-dollar sale means for collectorsThe watch's ownership history adds another dimension to the result. Phillips identified it as property of the original owner, and the catalogue dates the example to around 2021. Barrington Watch Winders reported that the owner had bought it new in 2021 before consigning it for the October 2026 sale. The $1.016 million result is a substantial difference from the auction estimate, but it should not automatically be treated as the owner's profit. The original purchase price, transaction costs, insurance, servicing and other expenses would be needed to calculate the actual return.The sale also does not guarantee that other Voutilainen watches will command similar prices. The 28Sport's limited production, unusual onyx-and-guilloché dial and condition as a complete set distinguish this particular example. Nevertheless, the result illustrates how independent watchmakers can attract significant collector interest when craftsmanship and scarcity come together. For a watch estimated at $240,000 at the upper end, a seven-figure sale represents a striking auction outcome and a notable moment for the Voutilainen 28Sport.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Shaurya commandos' prepared: ITBP chief flags ‘ongoing’ China faceoff along Arunachal border
articles.summary: The Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) has raised a new combat unit, the Shaurya commandos, who have demonstrated their capabilities during the “ongoing”
articles.body: The Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) has raised a new combat unit, the Shaurya commandos, who have demonstrated their capabilities during the “ongoing” faceoff with Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops at multiple locations in Arunachal Pradesh, ITBP chief Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor said on Thursday.Kapoor said the commandos would be deployed in every border battalion as the force strengthens its combat readiness along the 3,488-km Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The ITBP chief’s remarks came as the force steps up its modernisation drive, with a greater focus on emerging warfare technologies and specialised training.Addressing personnel at an ITBP base in Alwar, Rajasthan, ahead of the force’s 65th Raising Day on October 24, Kapoor said traditional methods of warfare were no longer sufficient to counter China, which he described as India’s “biggest adversary”.The force has raised drone platoons in all its border-guarding battalions and is training personnel to operate drones and develop the technology. Kapoor said the ITBP had received Rs 400 crore in government funding, with 70% earmarked for strengthening its drone warfare capabilities. The Ministry of Home Affairs has also given in-principle approval to a Rs 4,000-crore modernisation plan, including Rs 1,000 crore for drone and anti-drone systems.The ITBP has also developed a new ‘Strike’ course to prepare personnel for combat situations similar to the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash. Kapoor said the entire force would undergo the training by the end of 2027.During the Galwan clash in eastern Ladakh, 20 Indian soldiers were killed in a violent confrontation with Chinese troops. China later acknowledged the deaths of four of its soldiers.Beyond combat training and technology, the force is also strengthening infrastructure at forward locations. Kapoor said the ITBP was building underground shelters in border areas to reduce vulnerabilities in the event of a conflict, as above-ground structures could become targets during a war.The force is also upgrading troop facilities in high-altitude areas, including insulating barracks, installing solar water heaters and providing generator sets to ensure electricity at remote posts. It has introduced cold-start kits to help vehicles start in freezing conditions.Kapoor said these measures were part of a broader plan to develop the ITBP into a specialised high-altitude mountain-fighting force capable of responding to evolving security challenges along the China border.Congress targets CentreCongress MP Jairam Ramesh accused the Centre of making concessions to China and failing to address concerns over border tensions in Arunachal Pradesh. He also alleged that India had lost access to certain patrolling points in the region.In a post on X, Ramesh cited the Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) praising the force’s performance during recent face-offs with China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) in Arunachal Pradesh. He questioned the government’s silence on the reported incidents, alleging that neither the Prime Minister nor his establishment had publicly addressed the matter.The Congress leader also flagged China’s moves to rename places in Arunachal Pradesh and its reported construction of a 60,000-MW dam, "Local residents have reported that, just like in Ladakh, several patrolling points have once again slipped from our control. China is relentlessly renaming our towns in Arunachal Pradesh and constructing a 60,000 MW dam, which poses a major threat to our ecology and water security."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2005, a meteorite hunter found a 1,430-pound space rock beneath a Kansas farm; the landowner was due a share of a find valued at up to $1 million
articles.summary: In 2005, meteorite hunter Steve Arnold unearthed a 1,430-pound pallasite meteorite beneath a Kansas farm, leading to speculation that this extraordinary find could be valued at over $1 million. The rock’s history and geological significance make it a remarkable piece for both scientific study and collectors.
articles.body: Many meteorites are found on or near the surface, but a large, dense one can sit below the ground in a field for a very long time. Meteorite hunting often involves using a metal detector and obtaining permission from the landowner before searching the property. The hunter, the hunt’s financiers and the landowner usually agree in advance on how to divide the proceeds, with the final amounts determined when the meteorite is sold.The Brenham scatter field in Kiowa County, KansasThe Kansas Geological Survey’s educational site GeoKansas says that Eliza Kimberly found rocks on her family’s property near Brenham in 1882, which drew scientists and hunters to the area. All the samples are believed to come from one meteorite that broke up on its way down. The American Museum of Natural History says the Brenham meteorite scattered more than three tons of fragments near the town and that pieces have been found as far as 1,500 kilometers from the fall site, likely carried by Native American traders and later buried in Hopewell mounds more than 1,500 years ago. The same region produced a 1,000-pound piece in 1949, now on display in Greensburg, the Associated Press reported. The museum adds that the Brenham mass is famous not just for its size, but for its nickel-iron metal and green olivine crystals, which make it a classic pallasite.Steve Arnold’s find on Allen Binford’s farmAccording to the Associated Press report republished by the Houston Chronicle, Steve Arnold, a meteorite hunter from Kingston, Arkansas, discovered the rock in Brenham Township, Kiowa County, Kansas, using a metal detector mounted on a three-wheeled vehicle. The rock was buried seven feet underground. Heritage Auctions records October 16, 2005, as the discovery date of the 1,433-pound Brenham meteorite found by Steve Arnold and Philip Mani in Kansas. Initial reports described it as a 1,400-pound rock, but later weighing on a grain scale showed it weighed 1,430 pounds. The farm belonged to Allen Binford, a photo caption from the same report noted. Steve Arnold referred to the rock as an oriented pallasite because of its conical appearance and olivine crystals embedded in an iron-nickel alloy. At the time, only two larger oriented pallasites were known: a 3,100-pound rock in Australia and a 1,500-pound rock in Argentina.A landowner’s share and a value estimated at seven figuresArnold claimed to reporters that the rock was worth “in the seven figures,” while sources contacted by MSNBC.com felt that such a valuation was not unreasonable for pallasites. The Baltimore Sun put the value range at $600,000 to $1 million. Arnold’s expedition was backed by his partner, Philip Mani, a San Antonio, Texas, lawyer and geologist who helped finance the search, while the landowner was entitled to a share of the proceeds from any meteorite sale. Later reports named three owners: Mani, Arnold and Binford.At the Bonhams auction on a Sunday in late October 2007, the rock drew a top bid of only $200,000, well short of its pre-auction estimate of $630,000 to $700,000 and the auctioneer withdrew it from sale. Mani told the Associated Press that he was disappointed, but the owners were working on their strategy. The reports used here do not say what the three owners did next.What a 2002 study and a 2022 study found about Brenham’s exposure age and pallasite formationThe 2002 study, Cosmogenic nuclides in the Brenham Pallasite, calculated that the rock was exposed to cosmic rays in space for about 156 ± 8 million years before it fell. Regarding how pallasites form, the study Isotopic evidence for pallasite formation by impact mixing of olivine and metal during the first 10 million years of the Solar System, published on March 9, 2022, in PNAS Nexus, argued that an impact mixed olivine and metal. Its authors inferred that the impactor differentiated within about 1 to 2 million years of the start of the Solar System and that the impact happened between about 1.5 and 9.5 million years after the earliest solids formed. In addition to this, the above-discussed 2002 research discovered unusually low quantities of elements like potassium, uranium and thorium in Brenham, thus making it possible to study the origin of certain nuclides uniquely.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2010, Paul Walker started a disaster-relief group after the Haiti earthquake; more than a decade after the actor's death, the organisation's volunteers helped 13,093 people in 2025 alone
articles.summary: More than a decade after actor Paul Walker died, the disaster-relief organisation he founded continues to help communities affected by natural disasters.
articles.body: More than a decade after actor Paul Walker died, the disaster-relief organisation he founded continues to help communities affected by natural disasters. Reach Out WorldWide (ROWW), established in 2010 following the devastating earthquake in Haiti, reported that it impacted 13,093 people through its work in 2025, supported by 738 volunteers. According to the organisation’s official Our Impact page, its work focuses on filling gaps in emergency response, particularly when affected communities need immediate assistance before larger relief operations are fully mobilised. The latest figures reflect how Walker’s original effort has grown into a continuing disaster-response mission.How the Haiti earthquake inspired Paul WalkerWalker, best known for his role in The Fast and the Furious film franchise, founded ROWW after travelling to Haiti in January 2010, following a powerful earthquake that devastated the country. He assembled a team of friends and volunteers to provide assistance to people affected by the disaster. During the response, Walker recognised that communities needed more than donated supplies. Skilled volunteers, including medical professionals and people with construction experience, could help address urgent needs that might otherwise go unmet.After returning from Haiti, he established ROWW to organise similar responses to natural disasters. The organisation’s mission was built around deploying small, agile teams that could reach affected areas quickly and work alongside local responders. Walker participated in relief efforts himself rather than limiting his involvement to fundraising. His commitment helped establish the organisation’s hands-on approach, which continues to guide its work.How ROWW responds when disaster strikesROWW describes its work as filling the gap between a disaster and the arrival of wider assistance. Its teams include volunteer first responders and professionals with medical and construction expertise, allowing them to support local communities during the early stages of recovery. The organisation's work extends beyond immediate relief, with volunteers helping communities address urgent needs after disasters.Medical volunteers, including nurses and paramedics, provide care when local healthcare facilities are overwhelmed or difficult to reach. The organisation also distributes essential supplies and supports rebuilding work, depending on the needs of each affected community. ROWW says its smaller teams allow it to mobilise quickly and reach places that may receive limited attention from larger relief organisations. Its assistance is provided at no cost to disaster survivors, helping families preserve their resources for longer-term recovery.From Haiti to disaster zones around the worldThe organisation's work expanded beyond its initial response in Haiti. Its official impact page records deployments to Chile in 2010, the Philippines in 2011, Nepal in 2014, Vanuatu in 2015, Fiji in 2016, Indonesia in 2018 and the Bahamas in 2019. It also responded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and assisted communities in Oregon and Tennessee in 2021. In 2023, its deployment history included Turkey, followed by North Carolina in 2024 and California and Jamaica in 2025.These responses demonstrate how the organisation's original mission has developed to address different emergencies, from earthquakes and hurricanes to floods and other disasters. The specific work varies according to local conditions, with teams providing practical support where it is most urgently needed.What the 2025 figures revealROWW's official impact page reports that 13,093 people were impacted by its work in 2025, with 738 volunteers contributing during the year. These figures offer a measure of the reach of a programme that relies heavily on volunteer participation. The organisation also publishes annual impact reports and financial disclosures, allowing supporters to examine its activities and funding. Its approach places emphasis on practical assistance, rapid deployment and cooperation with local communities rather than measuring relief solely through money spent or supplies distributed.Walker died in a car crash in November 2013, aged 40. His disaster-relief initiative has continued through the organisation he established, with volunteers carrying forward its focus on helping communities recover after emergencies. The 2025 figures show how the effort that began with a small relief team responding to the Haiti earthquake has developed into a continuing operation. For ROWW, the central aim remains to reach people facing urgent needs, restore access and safety, and provide support during the difficult period between a disaster and long-term recovery.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1866, a monk printed 40 copies of his pea-plant research, but his discovery was ignored for 34 years; one rare surviving copy passed through a 2016 auction before selling for Rs 6.10 crore in 2026
articles.summary: A scientific paper that went largely unnoticed during its author's lifetime has become one of the most valuable pieces of scientific history.
articles.body: A scientific paper that went largely unnoticed during its author's lifetime has become one of the most valuable pieces of scientific history. Written by Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian monk whose experiments with pea plants helped establish the foundations of modern genetics, the rare 1866 publication sold for US$640,000, around Rs 6.10 crore, at a Christie’s auction in October 2026.The paper, titled “Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden”, or “Experiments on Plant Hybrids”, presented the results of years of carefully planned breeding experiments. Today, Mendel is widely recognised for explaining patterns of inheritance, but his findings were not fully appreciated when they first appeared. The auctioned copy also has its own history, having previously been sold at Christie’s in July 2016 before returning to the auction house a decade later.The monk who turned pea plants into a scientific breakthroughBorn in 1822 to a farming family in Moravia, now part of the Czech Republic, Mendel chose a life of study rather than following the family’s agricultural tradition. He entered the Augustinian monastery in Brno in 1843 and later studied at the University of Vienna, where he encountered scientific ideas that helped shape his research. After returning to the monastery, Mendel began investigating how characteristics passed from one generation of plants to another. His work involved cross-breeding pea plants and carefully recording the results.Over roughly a decade, he cultivated nearly 30,000 pea plants and studied seven pairs of contrasting characteristics. These included visible differences in plant and seed traits. Rather than relying only on observation, he used numerical analysis to identify patterns in how characteristics appeared among successive generations. His results challenged the idea that inherited traits simply blended together. Instead, they suggested that hereditary factors were passed on in distinct units and followed predictable patterns. These findings later became central to the study of genetics.Why the research remained overlooked for decadesMendel presented his findings to a local scientific society in Brno in 1865. The paper was subsequently published in the society’s proceedings in 1866. The work was also circulated as a separate printed edition, known as an offprint. According to Christie’s, 40 copies of this offprint were distributed to colleagues and correspondents at Mendel’s discretion, while the journal itself reached 134 scientific institutions in different countries. Despite this circulation, the research attracted little attention. Mendel’s ideas remained largely forgotten until 1900, when botanists Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently reached similar conclusions and acknowledged that Mendel had anticipated their discoveries.His work eventually became known for explaining inheritance through dominant and recessive traits, as well as the independent assortment of different characteristics. These principles helped scientists understand how variations could pass between generations and later became important to the study of evolution. The delayed recognition of Mendel’s research is now a striking example of how a scientific breakthrough can take decades to receive the attention it deserves.A rare copy with a history of its ownThe copy sold in 2026 is particularly significant because very few examples of the separate offprint are known to survive. Christie’s estimates that only 16 or 17 copies remain, including eight held by institutions. The 47-page publication was printed in Brno in 1866 by Georg Gastl for the local natural history society. The auctioned copy retains its contemporary plain yellow paper wrappers over a grey-paper backstrip and comes in a green protective clamshell box.Its condition is described as very fine, with only minor marks and faint creasing. For collectors, such details matter because surviving copies of foundational scientific works are rare and provide direct evidence of how important discoveries were originally communicated. The copy was sold at Christie’s on July 13, 2016, as lot 177, and acquired by its current owner at that auction. Its return to the auction market in October 2026 gave collectors another opportunity to acquire a publication closely associated with the beginnings of modern genetics.Why Mendel’s paper remains important todayThe sale price reflects the publication’s scientific significance as well as its rarity. Mendel’s experiments helped establish a framework for understanding how inherited characteristics are transmitted, a subject that remains central to biology, medicine, agriculture and evolutionary research. His findings were not immediately recognised, but their eventual acceptance changed the direction of biological science. The rediscovery of his work in 1900 helped connect inheritance with the broader study of evolution, giving scientists a clearer understanding of how traits persist and vary across generations. articles.title: In 2020, Mississippi researchers applied blue pond dye 4 times to control algae in catfish ponds; musty fish still appeared in 2 treated ponds before harvest
articles.summary: In a bid to address the age-old issue of muddy-tasting catfish, Mississippi researchers explored the efficacy of blue pond dye to combat algae in aquaculture. Despite multiple treatments, the results reveal that the approach fell short, with musty fish still present at harvest.
articles.body: Catfish aquaculture has a peculiar problem that most consumers never hear about. Processors taste a sample of the fish before harvesting; if the meat tastes musty or earthy, the pond is left unharvested until the taste goes away. A farmer with fish ready to sell has little to do but wait, and that can take days or weeks. The stakes are higher than they appear, because a customer who dislikes the flavour may not buy catfish again.One idea was to use pond dye. Some farmers wondered if the same approach might starve the algae responsible for the unpleasant flavour. A commercial blue dye called Aquashade is sold to control underwater weeds by reducing the amount of light that reaches them. Researchers from Mississippi tested the theory, and their results, published in January 2020 in the North American Journal of Aquaculture, were dismal. The colour did not stop the off flavour. In the study, fish that processors would have rejected as musty were found in two of three dyed ponds and two of three untreated ponds on the sample date just before harvest, so the dye made no difference.Where the musty taste comes fromThe taste comes from substances generated by blue-green algae. These are plant-like microorganisms that grow in warm, nutrient-rich ponds. The musty flavour is associated with a chemical called MIB, and the earthy flavour is associated with geosmin. The musty kind is almost invariably associated with one species, a filamentous-shaped alga known as Planktothrix perornata, which older literature refers to as Oscillatoria perornata, in the main catfish-growing area, the Mississippi Delta.Fish absorb these substances via their gills, skin and intestines, and the flavour develops in the flesh. Extension specialists say the taste can develop in minutes or hours, but it takes days or weeks to dissipate and longer for large, fatty fish in cold water. That slow purge is why farmers wanted a way to stop algal blooms before they started.What the researchers triedThe work was directed by Craig Tucker of the US Department of Agriculture’s research service and Charles Mischke of Mississippi State University, both at Stoneville. During the summer growth season, they applied Aquashade four times, at a concentration of roughly one part per million, once a month. The dye was applied to three channel catfish ponds, with three ponds as controls.Then the crew compared the ponds. The dye had no measurable effect on nitrite or ammonia levels, the number of extra hours of aeration required for the ponds, the amount of phytoplankton, which are the microscopic drifting plants and algae in the water, or fish production in the ponds. Algae known to produce smelly compounds turned up at some point in every pond, dyed or not. The more interesting question is why a dye that works on weeds had so little effect on this algae.Why the dye didn’t make itThe dye absorbs light in the orange and red part of the spectrum, at wavelengths of about 600 to 650 nanometres, reducing the light available to plants growing on the bottom. The blue-green algae that produce the smell are adapted to those low-light conditions. The researchers point to pigments other than chlorophyll and an ability to change position in the water, both of which help these species thrive in low light. They are therefore not much troubled by a dye that dims the pond. The study was limited, with three ponds in each group, so it did not answer all questions about pond dyes. But the result is clear enough for farmers to weigh their options. Shading the water neither prevented the off-flavour nor had any influence on fish productivity.What farmers still rely onA 1999 extension guide from the Southern Regional Aquaculture Center spells out the basic choices, and they are mostly practical ones. When the odour-producing species leave, the flavour disappears, so a farmer may simply wait, because algal blooms come and go. The most reliable method, it says, is to move the fish into clean water to purge the taste. The algae can also be eliminated with an approved algicide, although it warns that copper-based products are problematic because they can stress fish and deplete the pond of oxygen. Some of the products and rules it mentions may have changed since. More recent guidance from the Global Seafood Alliance likewise starts with taste-testing to identify the type of off-flavour.Farms also plan around the problem. Many keep fish of different sizes in each pond so that if one pond cannot be harvested because of off-flavour, then another is likely to hold fish which might be ready to sell. It is not an ideal strategy, the guide admits, but it keeps cash coming in. The Mississippi test shows that pond dye did not solve the off-flavour problem.You use AI every day. articles.title: A three-year-old police Labrador whose arrival and training were funded by a $25,000 donation found a missing 70-year-old hiker in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park; it was her second successful rescue in just two months
articles.summary: A 70-year-old man who went missing while hiking in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park was found by a three-year-old police Labrador named Trina on Monday.
articles.body: A 70-year-old man who went missing while hiking in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park was found by a three-year-old police Labrador named Trina on Monday. According to the Hawaii Police Department, authorities began searching for David Arai after he had not been seen for more than 24 hours. The dog eventually tracked him down about two miles from his rental vehicle, marking her second successful rescue in two months.Arai, who lives on Oahu, was familiar with the national park and frequently explored its trails. His son, Kaohe, told local television station KHON2 that his father often went hiking alone. This time, however, his absence led to a search involving police officers, national park personnel and a helicopter.By the time Trina found him at around 7.30 pm, the search had been under way for more than seven hours. Arai was lying slightly away from the trail, among bushes. He was subsequently carried to the trailhead and taken to Hilo Benioff Medical Center, where he received treatment for dehydration and exposure.Trina, a Labrador Retriever originally from Sweden, had helped locate an endangered teenager in Waikoloa, just a month earlier. Arai now hopes to adopt the dog if she ever retires from police service.The rescue operationThe search began after Puna patrol officers received a report about Arai at 12.16 pm on Monday. According to the police, he had last been known to be in the Volcano area, and nobody had seen him for over a day.Investigators treated his disappearance as an endangered missing-person case after considering his age and information gathered during their investigation.An important development came when officers found Arai's rental vehicle inside Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, which helped establish an area for the search.Personnel from the police department and national park quickly began to search the surrounding area, while the Hawaii Fire Department deployed a helicopter to assist from above.Officer Christopher Ross, who works with the department's Area II Juvenile Aid Section and joined the operation with Trina, told KHON2 that the conditions along the trail were difficult. Recalling how he first spotted Arai, he said the man was lying on his back in bushes, a short distance away from the trail itself.“The conditions were pretty bad going down that trail. And the first thing I noticed, I saw the top of his head, and he was slightly off trail in the bushes, like pretty much lying on his back,” Ross said.The officer also described Trina's reaction when they reached the missing hiker. The Labrador not just simply stopped after finding him, but it approached Arai and licked his hand.“We led up to him, just wanted to make sure he was okay, and Trina, when she got next to him, she licked his hand basically to let him know that we found him and that he’s safe,” Ross said.Who is Trina, the police dog behind the rescue?Trina is trained as a live-find human tracking canine, a specialised police dog that helps locate missing people. She is also described as scent-discriminating, which means she can follow the scent of a particular individual.Her work with the Hawaii Police Department involves searches for missing children and endangered adults across Hawaii Island.Ross spoke warmly about his canine partner after Arai was found, describing how much her presence meant to him.“I don’t think there are any words to describe it. It’s a blessing just having this dog. It really is. Like my last thought, last before I fell asleep, was that we truly have an angel on our hands," he added.Missing hiker develops special connection with TrinaAccording to People magazine, Kaohe said his father was extremely grateful to the police department, park rangers and others who had participated in the operation. He was especially grateful to Ross and Trina, whose efforts ended the search.After meeting Trina, he also became interested in the possibility of giving her a home once her working years were over. “And if she ever retires and is looking for an adoption, he’s open. He said he fell in love with that dog,” Kaohe said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Kristen Bell says parenting her two daughters is so hard that she cries weekly, and explains why she and Dax Shepard changed what they share about the girls online once they were old enough to be affected by it; 2 parenting lesson for parents
articles.summary: Parenting rarely comes with a neat script, but the teenage years can make the plot especially unpredictable.
articles.body: Parenting rarely comes with a neat script, but the teenage years can make the plot especially unpredictable. Kristen Bell is discovering that first-hand as she navigates life with daughters Lincoln, 13, and Delta, 11. In a recent interview with Bustle, the actor and mother recently opened up about the emotional highs and lows of raising children through puberty, admitting that even with years of parenting experience, there are moments when it all feels overwhelming. Her honesty also sheds light on another modern parenting dilemma of deciding what parts of a child’s life belong online and what should remain theirs alone.When parenting gets emotionalIn the recent interview with Bustle, Bell reflected on raising her daughters amid what she described as the “cyclone of puberty”. The actor, who shares her children with husband Dax Shepard, was candid about just how difficult this stage can be, acknowledging that she cries weekly.For Bell, one of the hardest parts is resisting the feeling that her family is somehow the only one going through a particular challenge. Puberty can bring sudden changes in mood, behaviour and communication, leaving parents wondering whether they are doing something wrong.Her experience offers a reassuring reminder that adolescence can be complicated for almost every family. Children are changing rapidly, while parents are simultaneously learning how to respond to a version of their child they have never encountered before.A new approach to sharing onlineBell and Shepard have also reconsidered how much of their family life they share publicly. When their daughters were younger, Bell was more comfortable posting cute moments and childhood memories. As the girls grew older, however, the couple realised that the equation had changed.Their daughters were now old enough to understand what appeared online and potentially have feelings about it. Bell has said that her primary responsibility is to protect them, which has meant becoming increasingly cautious about sharing their lives publicly.The couple have largely kept their daughters’ faces off social media, choosing instead to protect their privacy while occasionally celebrating family milestones.Growing alongside your childrenBell’s experience ultimately captures one of the less-discussed truths of parenting: parents have to keep adapting, too. What works during childhood may no longer feel right during adolescence.Her are two lessons that modern parents can learn from Kristen Bell and Dax Shephard.Parenting Lesson 1: Stop comparingDuring puberty, it can be tempting to compare children with their friends, siblings or even with how they behaved a few years earlier. But adolescence is deeply individual. One child may become more outspoken, another more withdrawn, while a third may experience dramatic emotional changes.Rather than constantly searching for whether a child is behaving “normally”, parents can focus on listening, staying patient and remembering that development does not follow a universal timetable.Sometimes, simply recognising that other parents are struggling too can make the journey feel less lonely.Parenting Lesson 2: Let privacy grow with the childA photograph that seems adorable when a child is five may feel embarrassing or intrusive when they are 13. As children develop their own identities, parents can give them greater control over what is shared about them. Bell followed that principle when she celebrated Lincoln’s 13th birthday with a montage of childhood memories while keeping her daughter’s face obscured.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amazon paid $427 million for a 122-acre university campus and proposed four data centres; after local opposition, it agreed to abandon the plan and pledge 25 acres for public facilities and $5 million for housing
articles.summary: Amazon has abandoned its plan to expand its data centre footprint in Virginia.
articles.body: Amazon has abandoned its plan to expand its data centre footprint in Virginia. The company was previously planning to build four data centres on a 120-acre campus at the George Washington University Science and Technology Campus in Ashburn, Loudoun County for $427 million. It has now withdrawn its application to develop the data centres. Instead, Amazon will donate roughly 25 acres of the property to Loudoun County for community facilities align with contributing $5 million to the county’s affordable housing efforts through the Loudoun County Affordable Housing Trust Fund.The agreement is called “Project Potomac Promise” by Loudoun County Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall. It calls for the e-commerce giant to withdraw its data centre site plan, abandon legal action to pursue development on the property, and work with the county to rezone the remaining land for mixed-use development.As reported by Fortune, Randall in a press conference alongside Amazon Web Services data centre delivery vice president Joshua Weissman said: “My goal was to disallow data centres or infrastructure that could support data centres on this property. Through our collaborative, respectful conversations, Amazon has agreed to forego its proposed application for data centres, and of note, forego any legal action to realize data centre development on this site.”How Amazon abandoned plan to build $427 million data centresAs stated in a Fortune report, GW president Ellen Granberg announced the university had sold the campus in February this year. However, she did not disclose the buyer or purchase price. The university then said the transaction would help support its “long-term financial health.” In March, the university’s student newspaper, The GW Hatchet, identified Amazon Data Services as the buyer, which purchased the property for $427 million.In July this year, Amazon filed a site plan for a proposed data centre development. Titled “Bridgefield Tech Centre,” the proposal asked for four two-story data centre buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet.Algonkian district supervisor Juli Briskman asked county staff to study the possible impact of the proposed project. She said Amazon’s $427 million purchase price, about four times the property’s assessed value, and the land’s zoning made it likely that the company planned to build a data centre there. However, by July, Briskman had raised concerns about adding another large data centre to the area.“Replacing the George Washington University campus with four massive data centre buildings would be a profound loss for our community,” Briskman said in a press release. “The site offers a generational opportunity for education, research, housing, and other forms of economic development that could directly benefit Loudoun residents. I strongly oppose this proposal and will fight it every step of the way.”Amazon eventually chose to work out a deal with Loudoun County and dropped its plans to invest in the data centre project.“There was not a moment where it was decided that this was a bad idea,” Weissman said. “We just heard from the community. We partnered with Loudoun, and we just decided this was just the right thing to do.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ohio lowered Guilford Lake by 20 feet for a $14 million dam rehabilitation project; the reservoir is expected to refill in 2027
articles.summary: Ohio has lowered Guilford Lake by 20 feet as part of a $14 million dam rehabilitation project to address structural deficiencies and meet modern safety
articles.body: Ohio has lowered Guilford Lake by 20 feet as part of a $14 million dam rehabilitation project to address structural deficiencies and meet modern safety requirements. According to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR), the reservoir reached full drawdown during preparations for construction, which includes replacing the existing spillway and improving the dam’s drainage system and embankment stability. The work is intended to help the dam safely manage major flood events and protect downstream communities. Construction was reported to be on schedule in June 2026, with the lake expected to begin refilling in winter 2026–27 and reach normal levels by spring 2027, weather permitting.Why did Ohio lower Guilford Lake for dam rehabilitationThe rehabilitation follows engineering evaluations that identified deterioration in the dam’s concrete spillway, including separation at its joints. The existing spillway also lacked sufficient capacity to safely pass the Probable Maximum Flood (PMF), the largest flood considered in the project’s design requirements. ODNR said the dam’s embankment had insufficient safety factors for seepage and stability, while its internal drainage system had reached the end of its design life.The department stated that addressing these deficiencies was necessary to protect downstream communities and preserve Guilford Lake as a recreational resource. The dam has undergone several major interventions since its original construction, including a full reconstruction in 1933 and modifications in 1957, 1968 and 1983. The current rehabilitation is designed to bring the structure into compliance with modern dam safety regulations and prepare it for continued service in the coming decades.How will Ohio’s new spillway improve Guilford Lake Dam safetyThe rehabilitation includes a new labyrinth spillway designed to pass the Probable Maximum Flood without overtopping the dam’s embankment. According to ODNR, the design is intended to maintain the lake’s normal pool elevation once the reservoir returns to its usual operating level. It is also intended to keep downstream discharges during significant storm events consistent with pre-rehabilitation conditions.Work on the embankment involves excavating the existing structure to install a modern drainage and filter system with monitoring capabilities. The embankment will then be rebuilt and reinforced with additional material at its downstream toe. In its June 2026 update, ODNR reported that the existing spillway demolition had been completed and concrete had been poured for both the upper and lower cutoff walls of the new spillway. Installation of a new toe drain had also begun on the eastern side of the spillway, while the stilling basin at the base of the structure was the next component scheduled for concrete work.What is the timeline for Guilford Lake’s $14 million projectThe Ruhlin Company was approved as the contractor after bids for the project were opened on 23 October 2025. ODNR reported that the project would cost approximately $14 million and that the state’s Controlling Board had approved the contractor and released the funding. Construction preparations included establishing a field office, installing perimeter fencing and signage, and putting erosion controls in place. A cofferdam made from sheet piling and water-control measures were also installed to allow the existing spillway to be demolished.Public access to the construction site remains prohibited, although the state park campground remains open. ODNR has stated that fishing is permitted outside the construction area, but swimming is prohibited throughout the lake. Vehicles are not allowed on the exposed lakebed, and the department has warned visitors to avoid ice because it may be unsafe as water levels change. The construction site is being monitored remotely, and periodic photographs of progress are available through the Guilford Lake State Park Facebook page.According to the project schedule published by ODNR, substantial completion of construction is anticipated in winter 2026–27, when the lake is expected to begin refilling. The department has identified spring 2027 as the target for completing the refill, subject to weather conditions. Although the lake will remain closed to the public during construction, ODNR does not anticipate long-term road closures, with most of the work expected to be accessed through the southeastern entrance. The rehabilitation is intended to address the dam’s identified safety deficiencies while restoring the reservoir to its normal operating level.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Archaeologists uncovered a 15th-century ship beneath Barcelona during car park construction; its wooden hull had around 30 ribs
articles.summary: Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a medieval ship beneath Barcelona’s former fish market during construction work for a new car park.
articles.body: Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a medieval ship beneath Barcelona’s former fish market during construction work for a new car park. The vessel dated back to between the 15th and 16th centuries and offered further knowledge about the city’s maritime history. Provisionally named Ciutadella I, the discovered section measured around 10 metres in length and more than three metres in width.Its wooden structure included around 30 ribs and at least seven planks covering the hull. According to Barcelona City Council, the remains, which had been covered in sediment over time, were in a very fragile state of conservation as of 2025. Archaeologists began documenting and preserving the structure to protect it from further damage.Medieval ship was discovered beneath Barcelona’s former fish marketThe ship was found during construction work for a new car park on the site of the former Mercat del Peix. The section discovered, provisionally named Ciutadella I, measured 10 metres in length and more than three metres in width. Its structure consisted of around 30 wooden ribs, which formed the curved frame along the sides of the vessel, and at least seven strakes, or wooden planks covering the hull.The remains had been covered in sediment over time and were found in a very fragile state. The discovery provided further knowledge about the diversity and complexity of medieval maritime activity in Barcelona, including the sailing and naval construction techniques used in the city during the 15th and 16th centuries.How did archaeologists preserve Barcelona’s medieval shipThe Barcelona Archaeology Service worked to document and conserve the ship after its discovery, advised by the Museu d’Arqueologia de Catalunya’s Underwater Archaeology Centre (CASC). The waterlogged wood was extremely sensitive, and drying could have caused it to fall apart. To prevent this, parts of the structure were covered with the original soil surrounding it.The initial conservation stage included three-dimensional documentation, labelling individual pieces, collecting samples, and preparing the remains for transfer into containers filled with water. The planned process also included desalination and the impregnation of the wood with water-soluble wax. The substance was intended to penetrate the material and strengthen its internal structure, helping ensure the remains could be preserved over the long term.What did the ship reveal about 15th- and 16th-century shipbuildingThe archaeological value of Ciutadella I lay in the information it provided about sailing and naval construction techniques used in Barcelona during the 15th and 16th centuries. The discovery added to evidence from another similar vessel found in 2008 near Estació de França. That ship was named Barceloneta I.The newly uncovered remains were being documented and conserved because of their fragile condition. Their wooden components and structure formed part of the archaeological evidence.How did the car park project connect research and sustainable mobilityThe excavation was linked to the construction of a 7,000-square-metre car park designed as a sustainable mobility services hub. The facility was intended to serve the future Barcelona Biomedical Research complex of the Spanish National Research Council and Pompeu Fabra University.The development formed part of the Ciutadella del Coneixement strategy, a scientific and urban project intended to turn Parc de la Ciutadella and its surroundings into a leading European space for knowledge, dissemination, research and innovation. The excavation also generated 40,000 cubic metres of sand from Barcelona’s subsoil. This material was used to regenerate Sant Sebastià beach through a joint operation involving the Port of Barcelona and BSM.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
